theory.intro: A prism can be drawn in 2 dimensions by looking at it from one direction at a time. The **front**, **back**, **side** and **top** views are the flat outlines you see looking straight at the solid from each of those directions.
facts: The **front view** and the **back view** show the prism's cross-section. If the cross-section is symmetrical the two views are identical; if it is not, the back view is the **mirror image** of the front view.
When a prism sits with its cross-section facing the front, the **side view** is a rectangle: as wide as the prism is long and as tall as the prism is high.
The **top view** is the outline seen from directly above, drawn with the length of the prism running down the page.
A view shows the outline plus a line **wherever the surface changes direction** — for example the ridge along the top of a triangular prism. Hidden edges are not drawn.
steps: Choose the direction you are looking from.
Draw the outline of the solid as seen from that direction.
Add a line wherever the surface changes direction.

foundation.solution_text:
From the front you look straight at the rectangular end face.
The surface does not change direction anywhere on that face, so the view is a plain rectangle.
[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.7]
\draw (0,0)--(2.8,0)--(2.8,1.8)--(0,1.8)--cycle;
\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]

Looking straight down you see the rectangular top face, with the length of the prism running down the page.
The surface never changes direction, so there are no lines inside the outline.
[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.7]
\draw (0,0) rectangle (3,2.6);
\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]

From the side you look straight at one sloping face.
Its outline is a rectangle as wide as the prism is long and as tall as the triangle is high.
[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.7]
\draw (0,0) rectangle (3.8,1.8);
\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]

The back view is the trapezium at the far end of the prism, seen from behind.
[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.7]
\draw (2.6,2)--(1,2)--(0,0)--(3.6,0)--cycle;
\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]
This trapezium is symmetrical, so turning it around left to right changes nothing: the back view is identical to the front view.

development.solution_text:
The front view is a triangle, so the cross-section of the prism is a triangle.
The line down the middle of the top view is the ridge where the two sloping faces meet, which is what a triangle-shaped cross-section produces.
The solid is a triangular prism.

The front view is a trapezium, so the cross-section of the prism is a trapezium.
The two lines in the top view are the edges where the flat top face meets each sloping face.
The solid is a trapezoidal prism.

mastery.solution_text:
Each prism has a ridge running along the middle of its top, so from above each one is the same rectangle with a line down the middle.
Each prism is also the same length and the same height, so from the side each one is the same rectangle.
Only the cross-sections differ: prism $P$ has a triangle and prism $Q$ has a five-sided shape.
The front view shows the difference between them.
